clue.text: Eggs found in a car

definitions.meaning: a batch of eggs laid and hatched together by one bird
the pedal that disengages the engine from the gearbox in a manual car

explanation.surface: Someone discovers eggs lying inside a parked car.
explanation.definitionFit: One word names both a brood of eggs laid together and the gearbox pedal every manual motor has.

clue.text: Comprehensive showing great understanding

explanation.surface: Praise for someone thorough who displays deep insight.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means broad in scope, big in size, and in older use generous or magnanimous in outlook.

clue.text: Tool can begin effecting repairs from the start

parts.note: a can is a tin
to open is to begin, as in opening a meeting

indicators.note: from the start means take the first letter of each of the words effecting and repairs

explanation.surface: A tool able to start mending things from the beginning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can' looks like a verb, 'is able to', but it is the noun TIN; 'from the start' takes E and R from 'effecting repairs'.
explanation.definitionFit: A kitchen gadget for cutting lids off cans is a type of tool.

clue.text: Bloom with colour coming up among the grass

indicators.note: among means placed within, so the reversed colour sits inside the dried grass

parts.note: hay is grass cut and dried for fodder

indicators.note: coming up in a down clue means the word for colour is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: a dye is a colouring

explanation.surface: A flower whose colour rises among the meadow grass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloom' looks like a flower, matching the grass, but it means prime; 'coming up' reverses the colour word because this is a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Bloom in the figurative sense of a peak of vigour or prime matches a time of greatest success.

clue.text: Cowardice can be helped by bedsocks

definitions.text: Cowardice can be helped by bedsocks

parts.words: Cowardice can be helped by bedsocks
parts.note: the phrase for losing one's nerve is read literally, as chilly toes that warm socks in bed would cure

explanation.surface: A mock-serious remedy suggesting that nervousness can be treated with warm night-time socks.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is 'Cowardice'; the rest pretends the idiom is a literal complaint of chilly toes, which bedsocks would cure.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes losing one's nerve before a commitment, a form of timidity.

clue.text: Poetic work surely can't be art when translated

indicators.note: translated means turned into another form, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A sceptic's claim that a poem loses its art in translation.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is Chaucer's collection of pilgrims' stories in verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaucer's collection of pilgrims' stories is a landmark of Middle English verse.

clue.text: Much less neglect

definitions.meaning: used as in 'he can't walk, much less run'
to leave something untouched and not interfere with it

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means 'still less' as a conjunction and 'refrain from touching' as a verb, two senses of ignoring.

clue.text: Lights part of letter up

indicators.note: up in a down clue means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: a serif is the small stroke finishing part of a printed letter

explanation.surface: Lamps illuminate a section of a letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns SERIF round. 'Lights' is a verb, as in lights a candle.
explanation.definitionFit: To light a bonfire is to kindle it, to set it burning.

clue.text: Two men of the century's first decade

parts.note: Edward is a man's name
Ian is another man's name

explanation.surface: A pair of chaps from the early nineteen-hundreds.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward VII reigned 1901 to 1910, so the adjective describes that decade.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective refers to the reign of Edward VII, 1901 to 1910, the first ten years of the twentieth century.

clue.text: It doesn't really make fast relative speed

parts.note: a grandmother is a family relative
a knot is a unit of speed at sea, one nautical mile per hour

explanation.surface: A family member whose pace is not actually quick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' looks like speed, matching 'speed' in the clue, but here it means secure, as in 'make fast' a rope; this tie is notorious for slipping.
explanation.definitionFit: This insecure tie is a reef tie crossed the wrong way, so it slips rather than holding a rope securely.

clue.text: Used bad language endlessly about quarrels

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the shortened word is read backwards
endlessly tells us to drop the final letter of the word for cursing

parts.note: to curse is to use bad language

explanation.surface: Someone kept cursing over disputes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' drops the last E of SWORE to leave SWOR, and 'about' turns that round.
explanation.definitionFit: Noisy arguments or disputes are called by this British word, rhyming with 'cows'.

clue.text: Liberal backing accepted by the wronged wife

indicators.note: accepted by means taken inside, so the reversed word goes within the other letters
wronged suggests something treated badly, so the three letters of the word the are rearranged
backing means going backwards, so the word for generous is written in reverse

parts.note: liberal in the sense of generous or plentiful, as in a liberal helping

explanation.surface: A betrayed spouse receives support from the Liberal party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberal backing' reads like party politics, but 'liberal' means generous, and 'backing' reverses that word; 'wronged' scrambles 'the' so the reversal can sit after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A supportive partner, especially a spouse, is the traditional sense of this compound.

clue.text: Glory in Ulster's regeneration

indicators.note: regeneration suggests something remade, so the letters of the province's name are rebuilt in a new order

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: A celebration of renewed pride in Northern Ireland's revival.
explanation.walkthrough: Ulster is the northern province of Ireland; its letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Brilliance or splendour, as in the shine of distinction, is a figurative synonym of glory.

clue.text: Feathers fell

definitions.meaning: the soft fine plumage of young birds, used in pillows
a fell is upland moorland in northern England, as are rolling chalk hills in the south

explanation.surface: A bird's plumage came tumbling to the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fell' looks like the past tense of fall, but it is a noun: a hill or moor, a sense also carried by this word (the South Downs are English chalk hills).
explanation.definitionFit: Soft plumage and a stretch of open upland share this word.

clue.text: Viewer right to switch to 26

indicators.note: switch means change around, so the letters of viewer, R and to are rearranged

explanation.surface: A television viewer has the right to change channel.
explanation.walkthrough: '26' refers to 26 across, meaning efface; 'switch' rearranges VIEWER, R and TO.
explanation.definitionFit: On a computer, writing new data over old destroys and erases it.

clue.text: Mountain man goes to an island

parts.note: Ben is a common man's name
Nevis is a Caribbean island, partner of St Kitts

explanation.surface: A fellow travels to an island.
explanation.walkthrough: The result is the highest peak in Britain, in the Scottish Highlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Britain's highest peak, in the Scottish Highlands, is a famous example of a summit.

clue.text: In love, girl married, of all people, Edmund

parts.note: Ena is a girl's name
our means belonging to all of us, all people
Ed is short for Edmund

explanation.surface: A lovestruck girl marries Edmund, surprisingly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of all people' looks like a surprised aside, but it gives OUR.
explanation.definitionFit: Being smitten or infatuated is being in love.

clue.text: A woman without a husband, some feel, must be warped

indicators.note: warped means bent out of shape, so the letters are twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: Some think a single woman must be twisted in outlook.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the legal term, from old French, for an unmarried woman or one with property independent of a husband.
explanation.definitionFit: In law this old French term means a single woman, unmarried, widowed or divorced.

clue.text: It encourages the speaker to try and try again

parts.note: to try a case in court is to hear it
a second trial, again hearing the case

explanation.surface: Advice to a struggling speaker to keep on attempting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'try' is the legal sense: a judge tries a case. The repeated cry is the cheer of approval in Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: This repeated cry is the traditional shout of approval for a speaker, especially in Parliament.

clue.text: Queen's standard is unlined

definitions.note: the 's stands for is, linking the definition to the wordplay

indicators.note: unlined means without lines, and BR (British Rail) are the railway lines taken away

parts.note: a standard is a flag, as is a banner

explanation.surface: A monarch's flag has no lining.
explanation.walkthrough: BR, for British Rail, stands for railway lines; 'unlined' removes B and R from BANNER. 'Queen's' is read as 'Queen is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne reigned as Britain's monarch from 1702 to 1714, so the name is a royal example.

clue.text: Go on eating one vegetable

indicators.note: eating means taking inside, so the numeral goes within the word for chatter

parts.note: to prate is to go on, chatter at length
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Keep on eating a vegetable.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is Irish dialect for a potato.
explanation.definitionFit: In Irish dialect this word means a potato, a root vegetable.

clue.text: Wife interrupts minister to cause a change of course

indicators.note: interrupts means breaking into, so the abbreviation goes inside the verb

parts.note: to minister to someone is to serve them

explanation.surface: A wife breaks in on a clergyman so as to alter his direction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'minister' looks like a noun, a clergyman, but it is the verb meaning serve.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden veer or swing away from a straight line is a change of direction.

clue.text: I s-save up to become a doctor of law

indicators.note: up in a down clue means the letters are read upwards, backwards

parts.note: the stammer is copied, so save, meaning except (bar), comes out stammered as B-BAR

explanation.surface: A stammering student saves money to study for a law doctorate.
explanation.walkthrough: The stuttered 's-save' tells us to stammer the synonym BAR as BBAR. 'up' turns I + BBAR round.
explanation.definitionFit: A Jewish scholar and teacher of the Torah and its law has this title.

clue.text: Rob — and consider carefully the money taken

definitions.meaning: criminal slang for ransacking and burgling a house
to ponder something, mulling it in the mind
a business's total sales income over a period

explanation.surface: Steal, then weigh up the takings afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: Three definitions: burgle (slang), mull over, and gross takings.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase covers burgling a place, mulling something over in the mind, and a firm's gross sales income.

clue.text: Always keeping books in list

indicators.note: keeping means holding inside, so the abbreviation for books goes within the poetic word

parts.note: e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, always
NT is the New Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: Constantly holding onto books in an inventory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'list' looks like a noun but is the verb, to record in a list.
explanation.definitionFit: To record an item in a register or catalogue is to list it.

clue.text: In April, I'm becoming a member

indicators.note: In tells us the answer sits inside the run of letters in the next words

explanation.surface: Someone joins a club in the spring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'member' looks like someone in a club, but it is a body part, an arm or leg.
explanation.definitionFit: An arm or leg is a member of the body, an old sense of the word.

clue.text: Bore a title difficult to efface

indicators.note: difficult hints at something awkward and twisted, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Bearing an awkward title that was hard to erase.
explanation.definitionFit: To wipe out or erase all trace of something is a synonym of efface.

clue.text: Become ambitious, for instance — about time, for instance

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the abbreviation is read backwards

parts.note: e.g. is the abbreviation for exempli gratia, for instance
tide is an old word for time or season, as in Yuletide
as, as in 'cities such as Paris', means for instance

explanation.surface: Aspiring higher, for example, at about the right time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns EG into GE. 'time' gives TIDE, the archaic sense kept in Eastertide and Yuletide.
explanation.definitionFit: To start having hopes above one's station is to grow ambitious.

clue.text: Brook to supply catchment for river

indicators.note: a catchment collects water, so the verb for supply holds the river abbreviation inside it

parts.note: to endue is to supply or endow with a quality

explanation.surface: A stream feeds water to the area that drains into a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brook' looks like a stream, fitting 'catchment' and 'river', but it is the verb meaning tolerate.
explanation.definitionFit: To brook something is to tolerate or put up with it.
